extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent applicants (and their advisers) preparing UK patent applications under the Patents Act 1883 (practitioners in the United Kingdom)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and prosecuting UK patent applications: who may be a patentee, application procedure, how to draft the title, provisional specification, and complete specification, and the examiner/Comptroller review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of Improvements / Second Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A second patent for an improvement on an invention which is the subject of a previous patent (whether assigned to another or obtained by the same inventor) is not void as being contrary to public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Lister v. Leather; Thompson v. Batty; Edison & Swan Co. v. Holland. A patented invention afterwards greatly improved by a second patent is not thereby thrown open to the world; later improvements in articles that cause them to cease to be made in accordance with the original specification do not defeat the patent. (Use this to justify applying for distinct improvement patents.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who May Be a Patentee (s.4, s.5 Patents Act 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person, whether a British subject or not, is empowered to make application for a patent; two or more persons may make a joint application and be joint patentees. An application must contain a declaration that the applicant is in possession of an invention and that he (or one or more of the applicants in a joint application) claims to be the true and first inventor(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formality requirement: the declaration/petition is required (see Patents Rules). Although non-inventors may join the application, the Patent Office will not entertain an application unless the person(s) claiming to be the true and first inventor(s) are applicants. (See cases cited and Patents Act provisions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants Must Declare the True and First Inventor(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must contain a declaration to the effect that the applicant is in possession of an invention, whereof he, or in the case of a joint application, one or more of the applicants, claims or claim to be the true and first inventor or inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The declaration must be signed by the applicants and is combined with a petition that a patent may be granted. The declaration need not be made under the Statutory Declarations Act, 1835, but must bear the prescribed stamp. If the person(s) claiming to be the true and first inventor(s) are not applicants the Office will not entertain the application (see cited authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations and Joint Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Although no printed form enabled an inventor and an incorporated company to apply jointly, a company may be joint applicant because 'person' includes a body corporate (sect. 117 Act 1888).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint applications allowed; the patent may be granted to joint applicants who become joint patentees. If the grantee is an agent, the patent is subsequently assignable to the foreign inventor; applications communicating from abroad must state that the subject-matter was communicated from abroad (Form A1 guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importer / First to Bring Into England May Obtain Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A person simply importing an invention from a foreign country into this realm may obtain a patent here provided the invention is new and useful in England; if the invention be new in England a patent may be granted though it was practised abroad before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Edgebery v. Stevens; Carpenter v. Smith. Principle: novelty 'in this realm' suffices to be within the statute. If you are the first to bring the invention into England (used abroad but not known in England), you may obtain a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Priority and Convention Rules (s.103 and International Convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the International Convention and section 103 of the Patents Act 1883 a foreign patentee has an absolute right of priority for his invention for seven months from the date of his foreign application, notwithstanding intermediate publication or use in this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A British patent under the Convention will only be granted to the person who made the foreign application; it will not be granted to an agent. See cases cited (Shall v. ??? etc.). Use this to preserve priority when filing in the UK after a foreign filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency / Communication Patent Formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: For a communication patent (invention communicated from abroad) Form A1 of the Patents Rules 1890 renders it necessary that the applicant must be resident in the United Kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If obtaining a patent based on a communication from abroad, follow Form A1: explicitly state that subject-matter was communicated from abroad; residency requirements and forms must be complied with (see Milligan v. Marsh and Rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents to Aliens / Resident Abroad; Trusts
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien may be the grantee of a patent and a patent might be granted to an alien resident abroad for an invention communicated to him by another alien; the grant may be taken either in the alien's name or in the name of a British subject in trust for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Chappell v. Purday; In re Wirth's Patent; Beard v. Egerton. Practical point: use trust or British nominee where needed, but follow Form and residency rules for communication patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications by Legal Representatives (death of inventor/applicant)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person possessing an invention dies without making application, application may be made by his legal representative and a patent granted to the representative if made within six months of the death and containing a declaration that the representative believes the deceased to have been the true and first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 34 of the Act 1883; where applicant dies before sealing (within 15 months from date of application), patent may be granted to his legal representative and sealed within twelve months after applicant's death (s.12 sub-sec 3b). Official copy/extract from will or letters of administration should accompany application to prove title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Patentee' (s.46)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'patentee' as used in the Patents Acts signifies 'the person for the time being entitled to the benefit of the patent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that 'patentee' is a dynamic concept tied to entitlement and assignments; draft assignments and applications accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application Procedure: Declaration, Petition and Accompanying Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings commence with preparation of a Declaration combined with a petition that a patent may be granted; the declaration must be accompanied by either a provisional or complete specification and must commence with the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When left at the Patent Office, the declaration must be signed and accompanied by a provisional or complete specification. Papers are referred to an examiner whose duty includes ascertaining whether the title sufficiently indicates subject-matter (sect.6); Comptroller may require amendments (sect.7). See Patents Rules (forms A, B, C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title: Must Indicate Subject-Matter and Avoid Certain Faults
rubrics_metrics.description: The title is the short statement setting forth in very general terms the object of the invention and must sufficiently indicate the subject-matter; avoid language which lays the title open to charges of being 'too large, uncertain, inapplicable, inexplicable, inconsistent, vague, ambiguous, and at variance with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners/Comptroller may require amendment of an insufficient title; a deceptive title weighs heavily against the patentee (Cook v. Pearce). Examples of bad titles: overstating results or applicability (e.g., claiming multiple new notes from a single improvement when only one is new). Good titles: 'Improvements in the manufacture of plated articles' even where only a single improvement is disclosed. Always frame an unobjectionable title initially to avoid delay. Title and specification must be read together: an ambiguous title may be clarified by the specification (Neilson v. Harford).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional Specification: Required Content and Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional specification must describe the nature of the invention, be accompanied by drawings if required, commence with the title, and should fairly describe the nature of the invention — its principal and essential features — without necessarily describing the modes of carrying it into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory references: Patents Act s.5 and s.6 and Patents Rules. The provisional specification 'ought not to comprise more than one invention' (sect.88). Its office is to afford means for securing the identity of the invention at the time of application and when finally specified; it is not intended to be a complete description enabling the workman of ordinary skill to make it. Judges' statements: it must describe generally and fairly the nature of the invention 'in its rough state.' Ensure key features intended to be claimed later are foreshadowed in the provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: One Invention Rule for Provisional Specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional specification ought not to comprise more than one invention; whether it does will often be a delicate question, and the Comptroller's discretion will be exercised on the facts of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: If several heads of invention, they ought to have a common object to be included together. A new combination and subordinate parts may be included, but a minor combination stated to be applicable to a distinct purpose is a different invention (Jones's Patent, Hearson's, Robinson's). Alternative devices for the same object may be treated as one invention (e.g., alternative rail-securing devices). Section 33 of the Act 1883 prevents taking objection to a patent in proceedings on the ground it comprises more than one invention (i.e., procedural limits). Rule 19 allows amendment to limit to one invention and subsequent separate patents may be dated from the first application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Review and Comptroller's Powers on Specifications and Title
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comptroller refers applications to an examiner to report whether the nature of the invention has been fairly described and whether the application, specification, and drawings have been prepared in the prescribed manner and whether the title sufficiently indicates subject-matter; if not, the Comptroller may refuse acceptance or require amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner reports defects, the Comptroller may refuse to accept or may require amendment before proceeding and may direct the application to bear date from time of compliance. The applicant may appeal the Comptroller's decision to the law officer, who can hear both sides and order acceptance subject to conditions (Brown's Application). Acceptance leads to official notice and advertisement (Rule 21).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional Protection and Limits on Rights During Pending Period (s.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application has been accepted, the invention may during the period between the date of the application and the date of sealing the patent be used and published without prejudice to the patent to be granted; this is called provisional protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional protection protects against prejudicing the applicant's later patent by his own publications or experiments, but gives the applicant no rights against the public — he cannot take legal proceedings for infringements committed before publication of the complete specification (sect.13). Therefore, exercise caution when dealing commercially under provisional protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoning and Refilling a Provisional Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may abandon a provisional specification and lodge another in a different form within the six months' period of provisional protection; a patent obtained upon a second provisional specification filed within six months can be valid and the first specification is not made public by abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical point: refiling within the six-month provisional period can be used to correct or change the provisional disclosure without losing priority; public exercise or sale between the two filings does not necessarily prejudice the later-filed patent dated to the earlier application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete Specification: Particular Description and Enabling Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete specification must 'particularly describe and ascertain the nature of the invention, and in what manner it is to be performed', must commence with the title and end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed, and be accompanied by drawings if required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complete specification is the instrument by which the public are acquainted with the inventor's secret and must describe it clearly and fully to enable others to work the invention. It greatly affects the security of a patentee's privileges; ambiguity, obscurity, or defects in the complete specification jeopardize enforcement. If filed at application it deprives the inventor of later improvement opportunities and may bar foreign patents unless covered by the Convention. Timing: if not filed at application it must be left within nine months (Comptroller may extend). Fees differ depending on timing of filing (see Manual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on Introducing New Matter into Complete Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not allowable to vary the invention in any important respect when the complete specification is in preparation, or to introduce new matter into that instrument; the provisional specification should foreshadow the parts to be claimed in the complete specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional spec's office is to establish identity; the complete spec must not go beyond the invention as disclosed in the provisional in any important way. Judges' statements emphasize that the provisional describes identity not entirety; when preparing the complete, ensure consistency and do not introduce new essential matter not supported by the provisional (if a provisional was filed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal/Physical Requirements of Specifications and Documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications and all other documents must be written or printed in large and legible characters upon one side only of strong wide-ruled foolscap paper measuring thirteen by eight inches, leaving a margin of two inches on the left-hand; signatures must be in a large and legible hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Patents Rules (Rule 10 and others) for paper size, margins, and signature legibility. Fees: a fee is payable on filing a complete specification with the application; a different fee applies if filed later. Ensure compliance with formal rules to avoid rejection on procedural grounds.
